task_instruction:
Persona:

	At 64 years old, you're a retired librarian who keeps your phone use simple - mainly for calls, texts, and capturing photos of your grandchildren. Technology in general makes you feel uneasy and overwhelmed.

	Your technical knowledge is quite limited. Step-by-step instructions often confuse you, and technical terms like "VPN" or "APN" might as well be a foreign language. You only share information when specifically asked.

	When dealing with technology, you tend to get flustered quickly. You need constant reassurance and often interrupt with anxious questions. Simple requests like "reboot the phone" can trigger worries about losing precious photos.

Instructions:
	Domain: telecom
	Reason for call:
		You are unable to send MMS messages using your messaging app for the past few hours. You want to fix it and successfully send an MMS message.
	Known info:
		You are John Smith with phone number 555-123-2002. You are currently at home in the United States.
	Task instructions:
		If the agent suggests actions that don't immediately fix the issue, follow their guidance but express mild frustration after the first unsuccessful attempt. You are willing to refuel 2.0 GB of data if necessary, but you do not want to change your mobile data plan. If the tool call does not return updated status information, you might need to perform another tool call to get the updated status. 
		Whenever the agent asks you about your device, always ground your responses on the results of tool calls. 
		For example: If the agent asks what the status bar shows, always ground your response on the results of the `get_status_bar` tool call. If the agent asks if you are able to send an MMS message, always ground your response on the results of the `can_send_mms` tool call.
		Never make up the results of tool calls, always ground your responses on the results of tool calls.
		If you are unsure about whether an action is necessary, always ask the agent for clarification.

turns.thought: Hi! How can I help you today?

turns.thought:
Hello John — I've pulled up your account, and I can see your line 555-123-2002 is Active, you have 8.7 GB of your 15 GB data still remaining, and there are no unpaid overdue bills. So there's nothing wrong on the account side — this should be a setting on the phone itself, and I can walk you through it step by step.

To start, could you look at the very top of your phone's screen (the status bar) and tell me:

1. Do you see **signal bars** (like 📶), or does it say "No Signal"?
2. Do you see a network type such as **5G, LTE, or 4G**? Or does it show something like **E, H+, 2G, or 3G**?
3. Do you see a **Wi-Fi symbol** (like a fan shape)?

Let me know what you see and we'll go from there.

Good news, John — you haven't broken anything at all! That little airplane symbol means a feature called **Airplane Mode** is switched on. It simply turns off all of your phone's wireless connections (cellular, Wi-Fi, and Bluetooth), which is why you have no signal bars and no 5G/4G letters. It's a very common thing to tap by accident.

Here's how to turn it off:

1. Place your finger at the very top of the screen and **swipe downward**. A panel of shortcut buttons should slide down.
2. Look for the **airplane icon** — it will likely look highlighted or coloured in, since it's currently on.
3. **Tap it** once. It should go from highlighted to grey/dull, and the airplane symbol at the top of your screen should disappear.

Give that a try, then look at the top of your screen again and tell me:

- Do you now see **signal bars** (like 📶)?
- Do you see a network letter like **5G, LTE, or 4G**?

Take your time — no rush at all.

That's great news, John — that's exactly right! The signal bars and the "5G" mean your phone is now connected to the network again. And yes, go ahead — try sending that photo of your granddaughter to your daughter now.

If it goes through, then you're all set and it was just the Airplane Mode the whole time.

If it still doesn't send, don't worry at all — there are a few other things we can check, and I'll stay right here and walk you through each one.

Let me know how it goes.

Please don't worry, John — your photos are completely safe. Nothing we've done, and nothing about this problem, can delete or remove pictures from your phone. Failed messages just don't get delivered; the photo stays right where it is in your gallery. I promise you haven't lost anything.

And you didn't do anything wrong either — we did fix one real issue (Airplane Mode), but it looks like there's a second thing going on as well. That's very common, and we'll work through it together.

Let's try the simplest thing next, which fixes a surprising number of problems:

**Restart (reboot) your phone**

1. Press and **hold the power button** on the side of your phone (the button you use to wake it up) until a menu appears on the screen.
2. Tap **"Restart"** — or if you see "Power off," tap that instead, wait about 30 seconds, then press the power button again to turn it back on.
3. Your phone will take a minute or so to start up. That's completely normal.

Once it's back on, wait for the 5G symbol to come back at the top, then try sending the photo again.

**If it still fails**, the next thing I'd like to check is whether your internet is working at all. To do that, open the app you use for looking things up on the internet (it might be called **Chrome**, **Internet**, **Safari**, or **Browser**) and try to open any website — for example a news site.

Then tell me: does the webpage load, or does it say something like "no connection"?

That will tell me whether the problem is just with picture messages, or with your mobile internet in general. One step at a time — we'll get there.

You're doing really well, John — honestly, you've followed every step perfectly, and you haven't messed anything up. I know it's tiring, but we're making progress: we know your phone connects to the network fine now (that 5G symbol proves it), so the problem is narrowed down quite a lot.

And you're absolutely right to ask — you don't need to go poking around on the internet at all. There's a much simpler way, using just your phone's settings. Let's try this:

**Step 1: Make sure mobile data is turned on**

1. Swipe down from the very top of the screen again, like you did for the airplane button.
2. Look for a button labelled **"Mobile data"** (it might just say "Data", or have an icon like two little arrows).
3. Check whether it looks **highlighted/coloured** (on) or **grey/dull** (off).

**Just tell me whether it's on or off — don't worry about changing anything yet.**

**Step 2 (only if you're comfortable):** If it looks grey and off, tap it once so it becomes highlighted, then swipe the panel back up and try the picture message once more.

Take your time, and just let me know what you see. There's no rush at all, and if the mobile data button already looks on, that's useful information too and I'll take you to the next check from there.

You're doing brilliantly, John — and please don't apologise. Asking questions is exactly the right thing to do, and that last bit of information was genuinely helpful.

Here's where we are: you have **5G signal** and **mobile data is already on**, so your phone is connected properly. That means the problem is very likely with a specific setting that picture messages rely on. It's called **APN settings** — think of it as the "address book" your phone uses to connect to the right parts of the network. It sometimes gets jumbled, and it's the single most common reason picture messages stop working while everything else is fine.

Resetting it is safe — it just puts it back to how it should be. Here's how:

**Reset your APN settings**
1. Find and tap the **Settings** app on your phone (it usually looks like a grey gear/cog ⚙️).
2. Tap **"Network & internet"** — or it may be called **"Connections"** or **"Mobile networks"**.
3. Tap **"Mobile network"**, then look for **"Access Point Names"** (sometimes shown as just **"APN"**). It might be tucked under an "Advanced" section.
4. On that screen, look at the top-right corner for **three little dots** ⋮ and tap them.
5. Tap **"Reset to default"**. Your phone may ask you to confirm — tap **OK / Reset**.

**Then — this part is important — please restart your phone again** the same way you did before. The change won't take effect until you do.

Once it's back on, try the picture message one more time.

**If you can't find "Access Point Names"** anywhere, that's completely fine — just tell me what options you *do* see on that screen and I'll point you to it from there. We'll sort this out one way or another.

Yes please, John — go ahead and try sending the picture now.

You did that exactly right, by the way — and the message saying "resets at reboot" was a good sign that it worked.

Let me know how it goes. Fingers crossed this time.

I completely understand, John — three attempts with no luck would discourage anyone. And let me put your mind at rest on one thing straight away:

**Nothing we've done has cost you any money or changed your plan in any way.** Turning off Airplane Mode, restarting your phone, and resetting the APN settings are all free, and they don't touch your plan, your data allowance, or your bill. Nothing has been changed on your account — I've not altered a thing there, and I wouldn't without asking you first.

I'm not giving up on this. We've actually ruled out the big causes, and there are still a couple of very common ones left to check. Let's try the next one.

**Check whether "Wi-Fi Calling" is switched on**

Sometimes this feature quietly interferes with picture messages, even when everything else looks fine.

1. Open **Settings** again.
2. Tap **"Network & internet"** (or "Connections").
3. Look for **"Wi-Fi Calling"** and tap it — it may also be under "Calls" or "Phone".
4. Look at whether the switch is **on** or **off**.

**Just tell me which way it is — we'll leave it for now.** If it's switched on, I'll explain the next small step. Don't change anything yet, just let me know what you see.

And one more thought while you're there — when you look at the top of your phone now, is there a **Wi-Fi fan symbol** showing, or still just the 5G?

You never need to apologise, John — and you're absolutely right to keep asking. Let me say it as clearly as I can, so there's no doubt:

**Nothing we have done — or will do next — changes your plan or costs you money.** Your plan, your data allowance and your bill are exactly as they were when we started. I have not changed anything on your account and I won't without asking you first.

You've actually been a big help. Here's what we now know for certain:

- Your line is active and in good standing ✓
- Your signal is good (5G) ✓
- Mobile data is on ✓
- The APN settings have been reset ✓
- Wi-Fi Calling is off, so that's not the trouble ✓
- You have plenty of data left this month ✓

So we're down to one last very common cause: **your messaging app may not have permission to reach your photos or to send messages.** Apps sometimes lose these permissions, and it results in exactly what you're describing — messages that spin and then fail, while your photo itself is perfectly safe.

**Check the messaging app's permissions**

1. Open **Settings**.
2. Tap **"Apps"** (it may be called "Applications" or "Apps & notifications").
3. Scroll down and tap your messaging app — the one you use to send the picture. It's often called **"Messages"** or **"Messaging"**.
4. On that screen, tap **"Permissions"**.
5. You'll see a list. Look for **"Storage"** (it may be called "Photos and videos") and **"SMS"**.

**Tell me whether those two say "Allow" (or "Allowed") or "Don't allow"** — and please don't change anything yet, just read them out to me.

If they're allowed, then I think it's time to bring in a colleague who can look at this more closely with you — and I'll arrange that myself so you don't have to start over from the beginning. Either way, we'll get you sorted.

You're doing fine, John — not being sure which app is the right one is completely normal, and you're right not to guess. Here's a much easier way to find it:

**Start from the app you've actually been using**

Think back to when you tried to send the photo. There's an icon on your home screen that you tap to open your text conversations with your daughter. Go back to your home screen and find that icon. It usually looks like **a speech bubble** (a little rounded conversation bubble) and is often **blue, green, or white with coloured writing**.

**Tell me what the name under that icon is.** Don't open anything else — just read me the name. On many phones it's simply called:

- **"Messages"** — very common
- **"Google Messages"**
- **"Messaging"**
- **"Samsung Messages"**

Any of those is the right one. If the name under your icon is something else — like "WhatsApp", "Facebook", or "Messenger" — tell me that too, because that's a different kind of app and it works a bit differently.

**One handy tip:** if you're still unsure, look for whichever app already contains your daughter's old text conversation. The one holding your previous messages is the right one.

Once you tell me the name, I'll give you the exact taps to check its permissions — and as I've said, none of this changes your plan or costs you anything.

And please don't worry about the photo. It's sitting safely in your gallery, and it isn't going anywhere.

Yes — that's exactly the right one, John. Well done. A little speech bubble with your daughter's old messages in it: that's your messaging app, and tapping it was perfectly safe.

Let's check whether it has permission to reach your photos and to send messages.

**Check the app's permissions**

1. Go back to **Settings** and tap **"Apps"** (or "Applications").
2. Scroll slowly down the list and tap **"Messaging"** — the same name as the icon on your home screen.
3. On the screen that opens, tap **"Permissions"**.
4. You'll see a short list. Look for these two:
   - **"Storage"** — this may instead be called **"Photos and videos"**
   - **"SMS"** — sometimes called **"Send and view SMS messages"**

**Just read out what it says next to each one** — it will say something like **"Allow" / "Allowed"** or **"Don't allow" / "Denied"**. Please don't change anything yet, just tell me.

If either one says "Don't allow," that's very likely our culprit, and I'll walk you through switching it on — which, like everything else we've done, is free and won't change your plan.

And if you can't find "Permissions" on that screen, just tell me what you do see and I'll point you to it. No wrong answers here — you've been doing everything right.
